BLOODBORNE PATHOGENS EXPOSURE CONTROL — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme Innovations LLC

ABOUT THIS BLOODBORNE PATHOGENS INFORMATION SHEET
This Bloodborne Pathogens Exposure Control — Information Sheet describes California's Cal/OSHA regulation governing occupational exposure to blood and other potentially infectious materials, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5193, as those requirements relate to the working relationship between Jordan Lee and Acme Innovations LLC.

It summarizes selected requirements of that regulation: which employees and work situations the standard covers, the written Exposure Control Plan an employer with employees who have occupational exposure must establish and maintain, the Sharps Injury Log employers must keep, the universal-precautions and engineering/work-practice-control approach the standard requires, personal protective equipment requirements, the hepatitis B vaccination the employer must make available, post-exposure medical evaluation and follow-up after a reported exposure incident, employee training requirements, and recordkeeping and confidentiality requirements for exposure-related medical records.

Acme Innovations LLC has identified Pat Morgan as the person with responsibility connected to Acme Innovations LLC's Exposure Control Plan.

This information sheet is not itself Acme Innovations LLC's written Exposure Control Plan, does not itself satisfy 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5193(c)(1)'s written-plan requirement, and does not determine whether any particular job classification, task, or workplace practice of Acme Innovations LLC's does or does not involve "occupational exposure" as the regulation defines that term.

WHAT TRIGGERS COVERAGE: "OCCUPATIONAL EXPOSURE"
California's Bloodborne Pathogens standard applies to all occupational exposure to blood or other potentially infectious materials (OPIM), as those terms are defined in the regulation, but by its own terms it does not apply to the construction industry. The regulation defines "Occupational Exposure" as reasonably anticipated skin, eye, mucous membrane, or parenteral contact with blood or OPIM that may result from the performance of an employee's duties — a definition that turns on what an employee's job duties reasonably anticipate, not on whether a particular employee has ever actually had such contact. "Other Potentially Infectious Materials" is itself a defined term in the regulation covering specified human body fluids, unfixed human tissue or organs, and certain HIV/HBV/HCV-related laboratory and animal materials — it is broader than blood alone.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(a) Scope and Application. This section applies to all occupational exposure to blood or other potentially infectious materials as defined by subsection (b) of this section."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5193(a) (Bloodborne Pathogens), 8 CCR § 5193(a), scope and application (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5193.html)
  "EXCEPTION: This regulation does not apply to the construction industry."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5193(a) (Bloodborne Pathogens), 8 CCR § 5193(a), construction industry exception (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5193.html)
  ""Occupational Exposure" means reasonably anticipated skin, eye, mucous membrane, or parenteral contact with blood or other potentially infectious materials that may result from the performance of an employee's duties."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5193(b) (Bloodborne Pathogens), 8 CCR § 5193(b), definition of "Occupational Exposure" (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5193.html)
  Known gap: This clause states the regulation's own coverage trigger; it does not determine whether any particular job classification, task, or workplace involves "occupational exposure" as defined — that determination depends on the specific duties an employee reasonably anticipated to perform, which this clause does not evaluate for any specific employer. The full definition of "Other Potentially Infectious Materials" in subsection (b) lists specific body fluids and other materials that this clause does not reproduce in full. This clause also does not address the regulation's separate definitions of "Blood," "Bloodborne Pathogens," "Contaminated," or the many other defined terms in subsection (b) that give content to other parts of the standard.

THE WRITTEN EXPOSURE CONTROL PLAN
An employer that has an employee or employees with occupational exposure, as the regulation defines that term, must establish, implement, and maintain an effective, written Exposure Control Plan designed to eliminate or minimize employee exposure — a plan that the regulation itself requires be consistent with 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203, California's separate Injury and Illness Prevention Program regulation. The Exposure Control Plan must contain at least the elements the regulation enumerates, including the employer's written exposure determination, the schedule and method for implementing each of the standard's applicable subsections, and procedures connected to the Sharps Injury Log. The plan is not a one-time document: the regulation requires the employer to review and update it at least annually and whenever necessary, including to reflect new or modified tasks affecting occupational exposure and changes in technology that could reduce exposure.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(A) Each employer having an employee(s) with occupational exposure as defined by subsection (b) of this section shall establish, implement and maintain an effective Exposure Control Plan which is designed to eliminate or minimize employee exposure and which is also consistent with Section 3203."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5193(c)(1)(A) (Bloodborne Pathogens), 8 CCR § 5193(c)(1)(A), duty to establish an Exposure Control Plan (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5193.html)
  "(B) The Exposure Control Plan shall be in writing and shall contain at least the following elements:"
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5193(c)(1)(B) (Bloodborne Pathogens), 8 CCR § 5193(c)(1)(B), written-plan requirement (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5193.html)
  "(D) The Exposure Control Plan shall be reviewed and updated at least annually and whenever necessary as follows:"
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5193(c)(1)(D) (Bloodborne Pathogens), 8 CCR § 5193(c)(1)(D), annual review-and-update requirement (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5193.html)
  Known gap: This clause states the plan's existence, required consistency with Section 3203, and update obligation; it does not reproduce the regulation's full eight-item list of mandatory plan elements in subsection (c)(1)(B), the employee-access requirement tied to Section 3204(e), or the separate solicitation-and-documentation duty owed to non-managerial employees responsible for direct patient care under subsection (c)(1)(E). It does not state whether any particular employer has adopted an Exposure Control Plan or evaluate the content of any plan an employer may have.

THE SHARPS INJURY LOG
The regulation requires an employer to establish and maintain a Sharps Injury Log — a record of each exposure incident involving a sharp, recording specified information such as the date and time of the incident, the type and brand of sharp involved, and details of how the incident occurred, to the extent known or reasonably available. Each exposure incident must be recorded on the log within 14 working days of the date the incident is reported to the employer.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The employer shall establish and maintain a Sharps Injury Log, which is a record of each exposure incident involving a sharp. The information recorded shall include the following information, if known or reasonably available:"
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5193(c)(2) (Bloodborne Pathogens), 8 CCR § 5193(c)(2), Sharps Injury Log requirement (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5193.html)
  "Each exposure incident shall be recorded on the Sharps Injury Log within 14 working days of the date the incident is reported to the employer."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5193(c)(2)(D) (Bloodborne Pathogens), 8 CCR § 5193(c)(2)(D), 14-working-day recording deadline (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5193.html)
  Known gap: This clause states the log's existence and the 14-working-day recording deadline; it does not reproduce the regulation's full list of required data fields in subsection (c)(2)(C), the confidentiality-of-the-injured-employee requirement in subsection (c)(2)(E), or the separate five-year retention period for the log, which is addressed in the recordkeeping clause of this information sheet. It does not state whether any particular employer maintains a Sharps Injury Log or evaluate the content of any log an employer may keep.

UNIVERSAL PRECAUTIONS AND METHODS OF COMPLIANCE
The regulation's baseline method-of-compliance requirement is that universal precautions be observed to prevent contact with blood or OPIM: where it is difficult or impossible to differentiate between types of body fluid, the regulation requires that all body fluids be treated as though potentially infectious. Building on that baseline, the regulation requires that engineering and work practice controls be used to eliminate or minimize employee exposure, with engineering controls examined and maintained or replaced on a regular schedule and work practice controls evaluated and updated on a regular schedule to ensure their continued effectiveness.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(1) General. Universal precautions shall be observed to prevent contact with blood or OPIM. Under circumstances in which differentiation between body fluid types is difficult or impossible, all body fluids shall be considered potentially infectious materials."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5193(d)(1) (Bloodborne Pathogens), 8 CCR § 5193(d)(1), universal precautions (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5193.html)
  "(A) Engineering and work practice controls shall be used to eliminate or minimize employee exposure."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5193(d)(2)(A) (Bloodborne Pathogens), 8 CCR § 5193(d)(2)(A), engineering and work practice controls (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5193.html)
  Known gap: This clause states the regulation's general universal-precautions principle and its general engineering/work-practice-controls requirement; it does not reproduce the regulation's detailed, procedure-specific requirements for needleless systems and needle devices, the prohibited-practices list in subsection (d)(3)(B), the sharps-container specifications in subsection (d)(3)(D), or the separate rules for regulated waste, contaminated laundry, and worksite decontamination in subsections (d)(3)(E)-(J), which this clause does not evaluate as applied to any particular workplace.

PERSONAL PROTECTIVE EQUIPMENT AT NO COST TO THE EMPLOYEE
Where occupational exposure remains after engineering and work practice controls are in place, the regulation requires the employer to provide appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE) — such as gloves, gowns, laboratory coats, face shields or masks and eye protection, and ventilation devices for resuscitation — at no cost to the employee, and defines PPE as "appropriate" only if it does not permit blood or OPIM to pass through to the employee's clothes, skin, eyes, mouth, or other mucous membranes under normal conditions of use for the time the equipment will be worn. The employer must ensure the employee uses appropriate PPE, subject to a narrow exception the regulation itself states: where the employer shows the employee temporarily and briefly declined to use PPE because, under rare and extraordinary circumstances, the employee's professional judgment was that its use would have prevented delivery of health care or public safety services or would have posed an increased hazard to worker or co-worker safety in that specific instance.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(A) Provision. Where occupational exposure remains after institution of engineering and work practice controls, the employer shall provide, at no cost to the employee, appropriate personal protective equipment such as, but not limited to, gloves, gowns, laboratory coats, face shields or masks and eye protection, and mouthpieces, resuscitation bags, pocket masks, or other ventilation devices. Personal protective equipment will be considered "appropriate" only if it does not permit blood or OPIM to pass through to or reach the employee's work clothes, street clothes, undergarments, skin, eyes, mouth, or other mucous membranes under normal conditions of use and for the duration of time which the protective equipment will be used."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5193(d)(4)(A) (Bloodborne Pathogens), 8 CCR § 5193(d)(4)(A), PPE provision at no cost and definition of "appropriate" (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5193.html)
  "(B) Use. The employer shall ensure that the employee uses appropriate personal protective equipment unless the employer shows that the employee temporarily and briefly declined to use personal protective equipment when, under rare and extraordinary circumstances, it was the employee's professional judgment that in the specific instance its use would have prevented the delivery of health care or public safety services or would have posed an increased hazard to the safety of the worker or co-worker."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5193(d)(4)(B) (Bloodborne Pathogens), 8 CCR § 5193(d)(4)(B), mandatory use and the declined-use exception (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5193.html)
  Known gap: This clause states the general no-cost PPE-provision duty, the regulatory definition of "appropriate" PPE, and the narrow declined-use exception; it does not reproduce the regulation's separate accessibility, hypoallergenic-alternative, cleaning/laundering, repair/replacement, or removal requirements in subsections (d)(4)(C)-(F), or the glove-specific and mask/eye-protection/respirator-specific rules in subsections (d)(4)(G)-(H), which this clause does not evaluate as applied to any particular job or task.

HEPATITIS B VACCINATION
The regulation requires the employer to make the hepatitis B vaccine and vaccination series available, at no cost, to all employees who have occupational exposure. Where the employer is also acting as the evaluating health care professional, the regulation requires the employer to advise the employee that the employee may refuse to consent to post-exposure evaluation and follow-up from the employer-affiliated provider, and if consent is refused, the employer must make immediately available a confidential medical evaluation and follow-up from a healthcare professional other than the employer. Vaccination itself must be made available after the employee has received the required training and within 10 working days of initial assignment, unless the employee has already completed the vaccination series, testing shows the employee is immune, or the vaccine is medically contraindicated for that employee.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(A) The employer shall make available the hepatitis B vaccine and vaccination series to all employees who have occupational exposure, and post-exposure evaluation and follow-up for bloodborne pathogens exposure to all employees who have had an exposure incident. When an employer is also acting as the evaluating health care professional, the employer shall advise an employee following an exposure incident that the employee may refuse to consent to post-exposure evaluation and follow-up from the employer-healthcare professional. When consent is refused, the employer shall make immediately available to exposed employees a confidential medical evaluation and follow-up from a healthcare professional other than the exposed employee's employer."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5193(f)(1)(A) (Bloodborne Pathogens), 8 CCR § 5193(f)(1)(A), no-cost vaccination and refusal of employer-affiliated evaluation (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5193.html)
  "(A) Hepatitis B vaccination shall be made available after the employee has received the training required in subsection (g)(2)(G)9. and within 10 working days of initial assignment to all employees who have occupational exposure unless the employee has previously received the complete hepatitis B vaccination series, antibody testing has revealed that the employee is immune, or the vaccine is contraindicated for medical reasons."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5193(f)(2)(A) (Bloodborne Pathogens), 8 CCR § 5193(f)(2)(A), 10-working-day vaccination timing rule (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5193.html)
  Known gap: This clause states the general vaccination-availability, timing, and refusal-of-employer-provider rules; it does not reproduce the regulation's separate exception for certain designated first aid providers in subsection (f)(1)(A) and its accompanying reporting and vaccine-timing conditions, the prohibition on conditioning vaccination on a prescreening program in subsection (f)(2)(B), or the mandatory written declination statement in Appendix A that an employee who declines vaccination must sign, which this clause does not reproduce or evaluate.

POST-EXPOSURE MEDICAL EVALUATION AND FOLLOW-UP
Following a report of an exposure incident, the regulation requires the employer to make a confidential medical evaluation and follow-up immediately available to the exposed employee, including — among the elements the regulation specifies — documentation of the route and circumstances of exposure, identification and testing of the source individual where feasible and permitted, collection and testing of the exposed employee's own blood, and provision for post-exposure prophylaxis and counseling as medically indicated. The regulation also entitles the employee to a copy of the evaluating healthcare professional's written opinion, which the employer must obtain and provide within 15 days of the completion of the evaluation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Following a report of an exposure incident, the employer shall make immediately available to the exposed employee a confidential medical evaluation and follow-up, including at least the following elements:"
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5193(f)(3) (Bloodborne Pathogens), 8 CCR § 5193(f)(3), post-exposure evaluation and follow-up (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5193.html)
  "The employer shall obtain and provide the employee with a copy of the evaluating healthcare professional's written opinion within 15 days of the completion of the evaluation."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5193(f)(5) (Bloodborne Pathogens), 8 CCR § 5193(f)(5), 15-day written-opinion deadline (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5193.html)
  Known gap: This clause states the general availability of post-exposure evaluation and the 15-day written-opinion deadline; it does not reproduce the regulation's detailed consent and testing sequence for the source individual and the exposed employee in subsection (f)(3)(B)-(C), the 90-day blood-sample-preservation option for an employee who initially declines HIV testing, the confidentiality limits on what the healthcare professional's written opinion may disclose in subsection (f)(5), or the information the employer must furnish to the evaluating healthcare professional under subsection (f)(4).

EMPLOYEE TRAINING ON BLOODBORNE PATHOGENS
The regulation requires the employer to ensure that all employees with occupational exposure participate in a bloodborne pathogens training program, provided at no cost to the employee and during working hours. Training must be provided at the time of initial assignment to tasks where occupational exposure may take place, and the regulation requires annual training for all employees to be provided within one year of the employee's previous training. The regulation lists specific required content for the training program, including an explanation of the standard itself, modes of transmission, the employer's Exposure Control Plan, the use and limitations of PPE, and hepatitis B vaccination information, and requires the person conducting the training to be knowledgeable in the subject matter as it relates to the workplace being addressed.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(A) Employers shall ensure that all employees with occupational exposure participate in a training program which must be provided at no cost to the employee and during working hours."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5193(g)(2)(A) (Bloodborne Pathogens), 8 CCR § 5193(g)(2)(A), no-cost training requirement (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5193.html)
  "Annual training for all employees shall be provided within one year of their previous training."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5193(g)(2)(D) (Bloodborne Pathogens), 8 CCR § 5193(g)(2)(D), annual retraining timing (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5193.html)
  Known gap: This clause states the general no-cost, initial-assignment, and annual training-timing requirements; it does not reproduce the regulation's full fourteen-item list of required training content in subsection (g)(2)(G), the additional training triggered by workplace changes under subsection (g)(2)(E), the separate additional training required for HIV/HBV/HCV research laboratory and production facility employees under subsection (e)(5), or the training-record retention period, which is addressed in the recordkeeping clause of this information sheet.

MEDICAL RECORDKEEPING AND RETENTION
The regulation requires the employer to establish and maintain an accurate exposure-related medical record for each employee with occupational exposure, maintained in accordance with the general employee medical record regulation, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3204. The regulation sets a specific, lengthy retention period for that record: the employer must maintain the records required by subsection (h)(1) for at least the duration of the employee's employment plus 30 years.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(A) The employer shall establish and maintain an accurate record for each employee with occupational exposure, in accordance with Section 3204."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5193(h)(1)(A) (Bloodborne Pathogens), 8 CCR § 5193(h)(1)(A), duty to maintain an exposure-related medical record (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5193.html)
  "(D) The employer shall maintain the records required by subsection (h)(1) for at least the duration of employment plus 30 years in accordance with Section 3204."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5193(h)(1)(D) (Bloodborne Pathogens), 8 CCR § 5193(h)(1)(D), duration-of-employment-plus-30-years retention period (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5193.html)
  Known gap: This clause states the record-creation duty and the duration-of-employment-plus-30-years retention period for medical records; it does not reproduce the regulation's separate confidentiality restrictions on disclosure in subsection (h)(1)(C), the shorter three-year retention period for training records or the five-year retention period for the Sharps Injury Log (both addressed only briefly, if at all, elsewhere in this information sheet), the access rights of employees and their representatives in subsection (h)(4), or the transfer-of-records obligations in subsection (h)(5) that apply if an employer ceases doing business.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT OF RECEIPT
Please sign below to acknowledge that you received this Bloodborne Pathogens Exposure Control — Information Sheet.

Signature: _______________  Date: _______________

Exposure Control Plan Responsible Person: Pat Morgan
Signature: _______________  Date: _______________

On behalf of Acme Innovations LLC:
Signature: _______________  Date: _______________

(A) Hepatitis B vaccination shall be made available after the employee has received the training required in subsection (g)(2)(G)9. and within 10 working days of initial assignment to all employees who have occupational exposure unless the employee has previously received the complete hepatitis B vaccination series, antibody testing has revealed that the employee is immune, or the vaccine is contraindicated for medical reasons.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause states the general vaccination-availability, timing, and refusal-of-employer-provider rules; it does not reproduce the regulation's separate exception for certain designated first aid providers in subsection (f)(1)(A) and its accompanying reporting and vaccine-timing conditions, the prohibition on conditioning vaccination on a prescreening program in subsection (f)(2)(B), or the mandatory written declination statement in Appendix A that an employee who declines vaccination must sign, which this clause does not reproduce or evaluate.

expectedJSON.body: Following a report of an exposure incident, the regulation requires the employer to make a confidential medical evaluation and follow-up immediately available to the exposed employee, including — among the elements the regulation specifies — documentation of the route and circumstances of exposure, identification and testing of the source individual where feasible and permitted, collection and testing of the exposed employee's own blood, and provision for post-exposure prophylaxis and counseling as medically indicated. The regulation also entitles the employee to a copy of the evaluating healthcare professional's written opinion, which the employer must obtain and provide within 15 days of the completion of the evaluation.

citations.quote: Following a report of an exposure incident, the employer shall make immediately available to the exposed employee a confidential medical evaluation and follow-up, including at least the following elements:
The employer shall obtain and provide the employee with a copy of the evaluating healthcare professional's written opinion within 15 days of the completion of the evaluation.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause states the general availability of post-exposure evaluation and the 15-day written-opinion deadline; it does not reproduce the regulation's detailed consent and testing sequence for the source individual and the exposed employee in subsection (f)(3)(B)-(C), the 90-day blood-sample-preservation option for an employee who initially declines HIV testing, the confidentiality limits on what the healthcare professional's written opinion may disclose in subsection (f)(5), or the information the employer must furnish to the evaluating healthcare professional under subsection (f)(4).

expectedJSON.body: The regulation requires the employer to ensure that all employees with occupational exposure participate in a bloodborne pathogens training program, provided at no cost to the employee and during working hours. Training must be provided at the time of initial assignment to tasks where occupational exposure may take place, and the regulation requires annual training for all employees to be provided within one year of the employee's previous training. The regulation lists specific required content for the training program, including an explanation of the standard itself, modes of transmission, the employer's Exposure Control Plan, the use and limitations of PPE, and hepatitis B vaccination information, and requires the person conducting the training to be knowledgeable in the subject matter as it relates to the workplace being addressed.

citations.quote: (A) Employers shall ensure that all employees with occupational exposure participate in a training program which must be provided at no cost to the employee and during working hours.
Annual training for all employees shall be provided within one year of their previous training.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause states the general no-cost, initial-assignment, and annual training-timing requirements; it does not reproduce the regulation's full fourteen-item list of required training content in subsection (g)(2)(G), the additional training triggered by workplace changes under subsection (g)(2)(E), the separate additional training required for HIV/HBV/HCV research laboratory and production facility employees under subsection (e)(5), or the training-record retention period, which is addressed in the recordkeeping clause of this information sheet.

expectedJSON.body: The regulation requires the employer to establish and maintain an accurate exposure-related medical record for each employee with occupational exposure, maintained in accordance with the general employee medical record regulation, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3204. The regulation sets a specific, lengthy retention period for that record: the employer must maintain the records required by subsection (h)(1) for at least the duration of the employee's employment plus 30 years.

citations.quote: (A) The employer shall establish and maintain an accurate record for each employee with occupational exposure, in accordance with Section 3204.
(D) The employer shall maintain the records required by subsection (h)(1) for at least the duration of employment plus 30 years in accordance with Section 3204.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause states the record-creation duty and the duration-of-employment-plus-30-years retention period for medical records; it does not reproduce the regulation's separate confidentiality restrictions on disclosure in subsection (h)(1)(C), the shorter three-year retention period for training records or the five-year retention period for the Sharps Injury Log (both addressed only briefly, if at all, elsewhere in this information sheet), the access rights of employees and their representatives in subsection (h)(4), or the transfer-of-records obligations in subsection (h)(5) that apply if an employer ceases doing business.
